title: The Basics
description: How a football game actually works, one concept at a time.

entries.explanation: A team gets 4 tries (downs) to move the ball 10 yards. If they succeed, they get a fresh set of 4 downs. If they don't, the other team takes over.
entries.example: It's 2nd down and 6 — meaning the offense has used 1 try and needs 6 more yards for a fresh set of downs.

entries.explanation: The orange markers on the sideline are connected by a 10-yard chain showing exactly how far the offense needs to go. Getting a first down is called "moving the chains" because the crew picks up the markers and moves them to the new spot.
entries.example: A 12-yard catch on 3rd and 8 moves the chains — new set of downs.

entries.explanation: The biggest score. The ball just has to cross the front edge of the end zone in a player's possession — the player doesn't have to touch anything down. Worth 6 points, plus a bonus try afterward.
entries.example: A runner stretches the ball over the pylon at the corner of the end zone — touchdown, even if his body lands out of bounds.

entries.explanation: After a touchdown, the scoring team chooses: kick the ball through the uprights from close range for 1 point (almost automatic), or run one regular play from the 3-yard line (2-yard line in the NFL) and reach the end zone for 2 points (riskier).
entries.example: Down 8 late, teams score a touchdown then go for 2 to tie the game.

entries.explanation: Kicking the ball through the tall yellow uprights on any down. Teams usually try this on 4th down when they're close enough for the kicker but don't trust getting the first down.
entries.example: Stalled at the opponent's 20-yard line, the offense kicks a 37-yard field goal (the 20 yards, plus 10 for the end zone and 7 for the holder's spot).

entries.explanation: The rarest score: the defense earns 2 points by tackling the ball carrier in his own end zone. As a bonus, the team that got tackled also has to kick the ball away.
entries.example: The quarterback is sacked in his own end zone — 2 points for the defense, and they get the ball back too.

entries.explanation: A game is four 15-minute quarters with a long halftime break in the middle. The clock stops for incomplete passes, players going out of bounds, scores, and timeouts — which is why a "60-minute" game takes over three hours.
entries.example: A team trailing late throws sideline passes so receivers can step out of bounds and stop the clock.

entries.explanation: Separate from the game clock: the offense has a countdown (40 seconds in college) to snap the ball after the previous play ends. Teams protecting a lead let it drain; teams in a hurry snap fast.
entries.example: The broadcast shows a small :05 ticking down — the offense must snap the ball before it hits zero or they're penalized.

entries.explanation: If the ball carrier drops the ball before being tackled, it's live — anyone from either team can recover it. If the defense gets it, possession flips instantly.
entries.example: A runner gets hit, the ball pops loose, and a defender falls on it: fumble recovery, defense's ball.

entries.explanation: If a defender catches a pass meant for the offense, possession flips immediately and the defender can run it back the other way.
entries.example: A cornerback jumps the route, catches the pass, and sprints untouched to the end zone — a "pick six" (interception returned for a touchdown).

entries.explanation: On 4th down, instead of risking a turnover on downs, teams usually kick (punt) the ball far downfield so the opponent starts their drive with worse field position. It's trading possession for territory.
entries.example: 4th and 9 from your own 25: punting pins the other team back near their own goal line instead of handing them the ball where you stand.

entries.explanation: How each half starts and how play resumes after scores: one team kicks from its own territory and the other tries to return it. If the ball sails into the end zone and the returner kneels (a touchback), the offense simply starts at the 25-yard line.
entries.example: After a field goal, the scoring team kicks off to the other team, whose returner takes a knee — offense starts at the 25.
